main.text: [III, 97] CHAPTER 30. [col. 335]
That the Hebrew word אנפה anapha signifies some very irascible bird; perhaps the زمج [zmj] zummag of the Arabs, a kind of eagle that has its name from anger.

Among the species of eagles there is one, unknown to us from other sources, which the Arabs call زمج [zmj] zummag, and barbarous writers zumach and zimiech. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter On العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] Alokab, or the Eagle: وهو نوعان عقاب وزمج [wa-huwa nawʿān ʿuqāb wa-zummaj] Of it there are two species, okab and zummag. Tardivus in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], p. 170: There are two kinds of eagle: the eagle simply so called; and another, called zimiech or zumach. And again: Whiteness on the head or back of an eagle is a sign of the better eagle, which is called ZUMMACH in Arabic, NAPAM in Syriac, Philadelphe in Greek, MILION in Latin. On these words Gesner remarks: Of these, you will find the Greek and Latin name of the eagle in no reliable author. Yet philadelphe is plainly distorted from the Greek φιλάδελφος [philadelphos]. That this bird was called by this name by the later Greeks, although I have not read it elsewhere, seems to me probable for this reason: no more fitting name could have been given to it, nor one that expresses its nature more vividly. For it is characteristic of the eagle kind to love solitude and to be entirely intolerant of all company. Hence, as soon as the eaglets are able to fly, the mothers ἐκ τῆς νεοττίας αὐτοὺς ἐκβάλλουσι, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ τόπου τοῦ περὶ αὐτὴν παντὸς ἀπελαύνουσιν· ἐπέχει γὰρ ἓν ζεῦγος αἰετῶν πολὺν τόπον. διόπερ οὐκ ἐᾷ πλησίον αὑτῶν ἄλλους αὐλισθῆναι [ek tēs neottias autous ekballousi, kai ek tou topou tou peri autēn pantos apelaunousin; epechei gar hen zeugos aietōn polyn topon. dioper ouk ea plēsion hautōn allous aulisthēnai]. So the Philosopher, book 9, chapter 32; and following him Pliny, book 10, chapter 3: The parent also pursues the grown young and drives them far away, as rivals in plunder, of course. And besides, a single pair of eagles needs a large tract to plunder in order to be satisfied. They therefore mark out territories and do not prey close by one another. Aelian, book 2, chapter 39: Κοινωνίαν τε τὴν πρὸς ἄλλον ἥκιστα ἐνδέχεται [Koinōnian te tēn pros allon hēkista endechetai], It admits no fellowship with others. Likewise: Ἀλλήλων ἀπῳκισμένας οἰκοῦσι κα- [col. 336] λιάς, ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ διαφέρεσθαι ὑπὲρ θήρας [Allēlōn apōkismenas oikousi kalias, hyper tou mē diapheresthai hyper thēras]; They nest very far from one another, so that they need not fight over prey. Yet the زمج [zmj] zummag of that kind is truly φιλάδελφος [philadelphos]: it delights in a companion, and does not usually hunt alone, but with a comrade joined to it. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: الزمج طاير فارسية دو برادران لانه اذا اعجز عن صيده اعانه اخوه [al-zummaj ṭāʾir fārisiyya dū barādarān li-annahu idhā aʿjaza ʿan ṣaydihi aʿānahu akhūhu] Zummag, a bird which in Persian is called DU-BRADRAN (that is, two brothers), because, when its prey escapes it, its brother comes to its aid. Alleiths: الجمز طاير دون العقاب حمرته [III, 98] غالبة تسميه العجم دبران ومن طبعه انه اذا عجز عن صيده اعانه اخوه علي اخذه [al-jmz ṭāʾir dūn al-ʿuqāb ḥumratuhu ghāliba tusammīhi al-ʿajam dbrān wa-min ṭabʿihi annahu idhā ʿajaza ʿan ṣaydihi aʿānahu akhūhu ʿalā akhdhihi] Giummaz (another copy reads better الزمج [al-zummaj] zummag) is a bird below the eagle (that is, like the eagle but smaller), in which redness predominates. It is called in Agem (that is, in Persia) DABRAN (or rather, as before, دو برادران [dū barādarān] DU-BRADRAN, that is, two brothers): it is of its nature that, when it cannot overtake its prey, its brother helps it to catch it. More recent writers say the same of falcons. Vincent, in the Doctrinale, book 16, chapter 156: In catching a heron two falcons are released together: one of them seeks the heights; the other flies low near the ground; so that the one may bring down the flying heron by its onset, and the other may take it when brought down. Of the same bird zummag, Sariph in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār]: هو طاير معروف يصيد به الملوك للطير [huwa ṭāʾir maʿrūf yaṣīdu bihi al-mulūk lil-ṭayr] A well-known bird which kings use in fowling. And Giulbaki: الزمج جنس من الطير يصاد به [al-zummaj jins min al-ṭayr yuṣād bihi] Zummag, a kind of fowling bird. Abuchatim the Andalusian, or Spaniard, also said: انه ذكر العقاب والجمع الزماميج [annahu dhakar al-ʿuqāb wa-al-jamʿ al-zamāmīj] that it is the male of the eagle, whose plural is zemamigio. And Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: زمج طاير يقال له بالفارسية رهل [zummaj ṭāʾir yuqālu lahu bil-fārisiyya rhl] Zummag, a bird called in Persian RAHAL. This is another name of this bird in Persia, different from the former du-bradran. And Damir: اهل البزدرة يعدونه من خغاف الجوارح وذلك معروف في عينه وحركته وشدة وثبه والمحمود منه ما كان لونه احمر وهو احد نوعي العقاب ويوصف بالغدر وقلة الالف لكثافة طبعه وقد يقبل التعليم ولكن بعد بطو ومن عادته ان يصيد علي وجه [col. 337] الارض [ahl al-bzdra yaʿuddūnahu min khghāf al-jawāriḥ wa-dhālika maʿrūf fī ʿaynihi wa-ḥarakatihi wa-shiddat wathbihi wa-al-maḥmūd minhu mā kāna lawnuhu aḥmar wa-huwa aḥad nawʿay al-ʿuqāb wa-yūṣafu bil-ghadr wa-qillat al-ilf li-kathāfat ṭabʿihi wa-qad yaqbalu al-taʿlīm wa-lākin baʿda buṭūʾ wa-min ʿādatihi an yaṣīda ʿalā wajh al-arḍ] The people of Albizdara (which is an Arab tribe) count it among those birds which are swiftest in seizing prey. This is shown by its eye and its movement, and the onset with which it rushes on its prey. Among them the one that is reddest is preferred. It is one of the two species of eagle. It is described as treacherous, but slow to learn, because it is stupid by nature. Yet after some delay it at last becomes capable of training. It mostly hunts birds near the surface of the ground. Of the same name, but of a different kind, is the bird زمج الما [zummaj al-mā] zummag of the water, which we have shown in its place ^{a)} to be the catarractes. For the Zummag, a kind of eagle, and the zummag of the water, or [III, 99] catarrhactes, rush upon their prey with equal impetus. Thus eagles are said καταῤῥάσσειν [katarrhassein], that is, to hurl themselves with force upon their prey, as well as the catarrhactes birds, which got their name from this. Hence Eustathius on Iliad 19: Ἅρπη δὲ, ἢ ὁ ἰκτῖνος, ἢ ζῶον ἄλλο ἀετῶδες, ὃ εἰς ὕψος ἀρθὲν εὐχερῶς ὅπη θέλει καταῤῥάσσει [Harpē de, ē ho iktinos, ē zōon allo aetōdes, ho eis hypsos arthen eucherōs hopē thelei katarrhassei]; Harpe is either the kite, or another bird of the eagle kind, which, having risen on high, easily swoops with force wherever it wishes. And Pliny, book 10, chapter 3: The haliaeetus, poising itself on high, and on seeing a fish in the sea, rushing headlong upon it, that is, καταῤῥάσσων [katarrhassōn]. In the books of the physicians there is much about remedies from this bird. An eye-salve from its gall cures dimness of sight. Its dung, smeared on, removes blotches and freckles. The dung of a man who eats its flesh is useful for palpitations of the heart. These things are to be found in Damir, Abenbitar and Alkazuinius. We have observed that the Greeks of a later age called it Φιλάδελφον [Philadelphon] from its character. The Arabic name زمج [zmj] zummag suggests that it is irascible, since it is formed from anger. For in Arabic زمج zamigia is to be angry, زمج zamag anger, مزمج musinig angry. From this you may infer by a very probable conjecture that the Hebrew אנפה anapha (the species of bird which Moses lists after חסידה hasidah) is the very same as the Arabic زمج [zmj] zummag. For the אנפה anapha too is believed to be an irascible bird, because the Hebrew verb אנף anaph means to be angry, and the contracted noun אף aph means anger or wrath. Thus in Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] it is said to be so called שיתאנף מהרה, because it is easily angered. And in the Talmudic tractate Cholin, ch. 3, p. 63a, the Hebrews define it as דיה רגזנית, the irascible vulture. For it has been proved above ^{b)} that vultures are often confused with eagles. But, you will say, a reason is added why it is called anapha which agrees little with the nature of the zummag: למה נקרא שמה אנפה שמתאנפת עם חברותיה, Why is it called anapha, a name taken from anger? Because it is angry with its companions. The zummag, on the contrary, is Φιλάδελφος [Philadelphos], and admits its brother, or mate, into partnership in the prey. I answer that it may happen that those who were harmonious and of one mind in the hunt fall out with one another in dividing the prey, and are provoked to anger against each other.
The name ἀνόπαια [anopaia] could also have been derived from אנפה anapha; Homer uses it for a species of eagle when he says of Minerva, Odyss. ά. line 320:
Ὄρνις δ᾽ ὡς ἀνόπαια διέπτατο, [Ornis d' hōs anopaia dieptato,]

Like an anopaea bird she flew away. On this passage Eustathius says: Ἀνόπαια, εἶδός τινες ὀρνέου λέγουσιν ἀετώδους Φήνῃ ἐοικότος· [Anopaia, eidos tines orneou legousin aetōdous Phēnē eoikotos;] Anopaea, as some report, is a species of bird of the eagle kind, similar to the ossifrage. Others hold that Minerva is compared [col. 338] [III, 100] with this bird διὰ τὸ ὡς ὄρνις ταχέως ὁρμῆσαι [dia to hōs ornis tacheōs hormēsai], because like a bird she rushes swiftly, as the old Scholiast has it. This would fit best if the bird ἀνόπαια [anopaia] were the same as אנפה anapha, or زمج [zummaj] zummag. For the Arabs say this is من خفاف الجوارح [min khifāf al-jawāriḥ] among the swiftest of birds of prey. Yet the bird زمج [zummaj] zummag does not seem to have been known to the Greeks, since its description occurs neither in Aristotle nor anywhere in other authors. But I would think that the Phoenicians who crossed into Greece with Cadmus called by the name אנפה anapha another bird similar to it, which was called in Greek ἀνόπαια [anopaia].

There is a kind of falcon which is called montanus [mountain falcon], by the barbarians montanarius, about which Albertus says: Its body is short and very thick, and the tail especially so. The breast is quite round and large; the legs are strong and short in proportion to the body; the feet knotty; the talons strong. It is accustomed to look at its feet frequently. On the back and the outside of the wings the colour is ash-grey, which gradually becomes ever clearer and paler the more often it has moulted, with a moderate dusky variegation interspersed. The name anapha would suit this falcon best, because no bird is more prone to anger, if we believe Albertus, whose words are: This kind of falcon is wild and endowed with bad habits, irascible, of inconstant anger. Thus a falconer who has sufficiently understood its habits is rare. He adds that it should seldom be held on the hand, except at dawn, at the time of hunting, and when it is to be fed. For thus it grows gentle toward the falconer's hand as toward a benefactor, and lays aside its anger. Likewise: When it is angry, let the falconer not resist it much, for thus its anger subsides more quickly. And again: If the prey escapes, it is indignant beyond all others, so that in its anger it sometimes attacks the one calling it back, and tears the head or face of the falconer, or of the horse on which he sits. He adds: There are times when one falcon attacks another; in this case a patient falconer is required, who does not oppose it, but patiently refrains from calling it back until, its anger laid aside, the falcon's spirit grows gentle. And shortly after: Having laid aside its anger, it will return of its own accord to the falconer's house. And further below: If it grows immoderately heated through anger, it hurls itself to its death, which some of our companions had already observed to have happened in the Alps. Likewise: When a mountain falcon, coming from a crag, was pursuing a partridge, and an eagle, chancing to fly up from the opposite side, had snatched it from it, and the falcon could not wrest it back from the eagle, after trying in vain for some time it at last mounted very high and, making a downward rush and striking the eagle's head, killed itself and the eagle alike. One must therefore always take care that it does not fall into so great a rage. It is more common than the other falcons, and delights wonderfully in its own ferocity. Thus falcons of this kind are often found for whom it is not enough to have wounded and brought down one bird, but who seem to glory in bringing down many. And sometimes they so indulge their cruelty that, busied with killing birds, they forget their food. So Albertus^{R1} [III, 101] in Gesner, who hewed and smoothed what was crude in his language. From this description it appears that there is no bird, indeed no animal at all, more irascible than this falcon. But whether this bird was known long ago in the East is rightly doubted. Albertus indeed cites some things about this very bird from a king of Egypt, Ptolemy. It is a precept, he says, of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, that it should seldom be held on the hand. Likewise: Ptolemy instructs the diligent falconer not to release this falcon too often against strong birds. But these precepts of Ptolemy are as clumsily fabricated as the Epistle, bandied about today, of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, on the various kinds of falcons and their diseases and [col. 339] remedies. Its very title amply refutes it: for Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion were neither contemporaries of one another nor of the Ptolemies, but lived one or two centuries later; nor did they devote themselves to the art of fowling, but to the study of letters and the translation of the Bible. What of the fact that we have already proved above ^{c)} that this art is much more recent? Yet they are made to cite writings of the ancients, as if the ancients had written on the art of fowling long before.

Now, if one also wishes to hear the conjectures of others, in the Thesaurus of Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] alone ten interpretations of this word are to be found. "A bird," he says, "which some call the magpie, others the kite; Jerome, following the Greeks, the charadrius. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] says that it is דיה רגזנית, an irritable kite (rather, vulture). And it seems to me, he says, that it is what they call הירון heron, in Latin ardea. The Targum has אבו (ibbu), the kite, as some interpret it. You might also say the angry magpie. Some hold it to be the wood pigeon, others the woodpecker, others the jackdaw. Some of the more recent writers think it is the otus, of which Aristotle speaks in the History, book 8, chapter 12, which is so called from the little feathers standing out around its ears, as if eared. Some believe it is the hoopoe, because it comes closest to the charadrius, since it seems to bear a crest on its forehead." So says Pagninus, or Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs], who enlarged that Thesaurus considerably. And a third person could add much to both. For they had not seen the Syriac, which retains the Hebrew word, which Ferrarius's Syriac Lexicon explains as the porphyrio. Nor the Samaritan, in which anapha is ࠏࠎࠍࠉࠕࠀ [עסניתא], swallow. For Ajin stands there for Cheth, guttural for guttural, which is frequent in that translator. Nor the Arabic translators, of whom the two printed ones have here الببغا [al-babghā] albabga, or الببجة [al-babja] albabgia, the parrot, which the Greeks today call παπαγὰς [papagas], a word very like our own; and the two manuscripts العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] [III, 102] alokab, that is, eagle. Finally, of the three Chaldee versions they cite only one, namely Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos], by whom anapha is rendered אבו ibbu; but by the Jerusalem Targum it is rendered אבניתא abnitha (explaining the obscure by the more obscure), and by Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] דייתא אכמתא, black vulture. From this examination of the versions one may at least gather that the ancient translators had nothing certain about the true meaning of this word.

I will, however, say what seems to have moved Castellio, Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], the French, English, Italians, etc., to interpret it with R. Selomo as heron. Aelian, History, book 5, chapter 36, to prove that the starry heron (asterias), tamed in Egypt, understands human speech to some extent, says: Εἴ τις αὐτὸν ὀνειδίζων δοῦλον εἴποι, ὅδε ὀργίζεται· καὶ εἴ τις ὄκνον καλέσειεν αὐτὸν, ὅδε βρενθύεται, καὶ ἀγανακτεῖ, ὡς καὶ εἰς ἀγεννὲς σκωπτόμενος, καὶ εἰς ἀργίαν εὐθυνόμενος [Ei tis auton oneidizōn doulon eipoi, hode orgizetai; kai ei tis oknon kaleseien auton, hode brenthyetai, kai aganaktei, hōs kai eis agennes skōptomenos, kai eis argian euthynomenos]; If someone abusively calls it a slave, it grows angry; and it is incensed and indignant at one who calls it lazy, as though low birth and sloth were being thrown at it in mockery. If there is any truth in this story, the heron was provoked not so much by the word as by the gesture of the one abusing it. However that may be, the vain and powerless anger of the heron is in no way to be compared with the anger of birds of prey, such as the eagle or the hawk, which, at the slightest provocation, at once swell with bile, blaze up, are all in a ferment, and strike with beak and talons. It is therefore certain that the name anapha, taken from anger, suits the heron far less than a bird of prey.

Let the same judgement be passed on those who translate it woodpecker, because Ovid writes in the Metamorphoses, book 14, fable 7, of Picus, king of Latium, recently changed by Circe's sorcery into the bird picus,
And, indignant that he had suddenly joined the Latin woods as a new bird, he strikes the wild oaks with his hard beak, and in anger wounds the long branches. [col. 340]

It is clear that the poet said this to serve his scene. For otherwise the Martius woodpecker, in Greek δρυοκολάπτης [dryokolaptēs], does not peck trees with its beak out of anger, but τῶν σκωλήκων, καὶ σκνιπῶν ἕνεκεν, ἵν᾽ ἐξίωσιν [tōn skōlēkōn, kai sknipōn heneken, hin᾽ exiōsin], for the sake of worms and gnats, so that they come out, as the Philosopher writes in the History, book 9, chapter 9. This, of course, is the food it lives on.

But why should the otus be called anapha, since it is not irascible, but κόβαλος [kobalos] and μιμητὴς [mimētēs], a buffoon and mimic, so that it is caught ἀντορχούμενος [antorchoumenos], dancing in turn opposite one who dances, as the Philosopher teaches in the History, book 8, chapter 12? But neither is there anyone for whom anapha is the otus, as Mercerus thought. Only the Jews of Germany render it in their language trapp, that is, the otis [bustard], not the otus:

[III, 103] which birds differ greatly. For the otus is a nocturnal bird, ὅμοιος ταῖς γλαυξὶ, καὶ περὶ τὰ ὦτα πτερύγια ἔχων, ἔνιοι δὲ αὐτὸν νυκτικόρακα καλοῦσιν [homoios tais glauxi, kai peri ta ōta pterygia echōn, enioi de auton nyktikoraka kalousin], like the little owl, having little feathers around its ears, which is why it is called otus): some call it the night raven. But the otis, called tarda by others, is a species of wild fowl, in Arabic حباري [ḥubārá] hubara, which has already been treated ^{d)}. And this bird is indeed melancholy; hence the Arabs say كمد من الحباري [kamad min al-ḥubārá] more melancholy than the otis for 'extremely melancholy'; yet it is not irascible. Gesner describes it as very timid and faint-hearted, so that it dies even if only slightly wounded. Such great faint-heartedness can hardly coexist with irascibility, for anger is the whetstone of courage. Therefore I cannot at all understand why the Jews would have the anapha be the otis, especially since it is a species of fowl, and all species of fowl are held to be clean.

To pursue the rest in the same way would be lengthy and of little use. So we shall add only two points, less obvious: why for anapha the Greeks, whom Jerome follows, have χαραδριὸν [charadrion], and the printed Arabic has ببغا [babghā] or ببغاة [babghāh], parrot. The charadrius, as is well known, got its name from αἱ χαράδραι [hai charadrai], that is, clefts near rivers and torrents, in which this bird nests. Hence the Philosopher, History, book 9, chapter 11: Τὰς δὲ οἰκήσεις οἱ μὲν περὶ τὰς χαράδρας, οἱ δὲ χηραμοὺς ποιοῦνται, καὶ πέτρας, οἷον ὁ καλούμενος χαραδριός [Tas de oikēseis hoi men peri tas charadras, hoi de chēramous poiountai, kai petras, hoion ho kaloumenos charadrios]. Gaza rendered this thus: Others (birds) inhabit rugged places, rocks and caves, like the one we call charadrius from the steep beds of torrents, as if you were to say cleft-dweller. And the Scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds: Ὠνοματοπεποίηται τὸ ὄρνεον παρὰ τὸ ἐν ταῖς χαράδραις διατρίβειν [Ōnomatopepoiētai to orneon para to en tais charadrais diatribein]. That bird is so called because it lives in clefts along river banks. Accordingly, when in the Comic poet the birds were building the city of Nephelococcygia in the clouds,
Ὕδωρ ἐφόρουν κάτωθεν ἐς τὸν ἀέρα Οἱ χαραδριοὶ, καὶ τ᾽ ἄλλα ποτάμι᾽ ὄρνεα, [Hydōr ephoroun katōthen es ton aera / Hoi charadrioi, kai t' alla potami' ornea,]

The charadrii and the other river birds carried water from below into the air. Now, to this name charadrius there corresponds not אנפה anapha but אגפה agapha, which is how we conjecture the Greek translators read it, with Nun and Gimel interchanged, letters which are very similar. For אגף agaph in a bird is the wing, in a man the arm, in a river or channel the bank. As in Bava Bathra ch. 6, fol. 99b: ואמה מכאן ואמה מכאן לאגפיה, And a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side, at its banks. Hence Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh]: פירוש אגפיה גדותיה כדכתיב והירדן מלא על כל גדותיו אגפיים ראשונים בעופות ושניים באדם ושלשים בנהר ופתרון אחד להם. The sense is that the word אגפיה is the same as גרותיה, its banks; as when in Ios. III, 15 [col. 341]

[III, 104] the river Jordan is read to have overflowed all its banks. And that אגפיים is used first of birds for wings; second of man for arms; third of a river for banks; yet in such a way that by analogy these three mean the same thing, because banks are to a river what wings are to a bird and arms to a man, that is, equally on either side. Since, therefore, the word אגף agaph was in use among the Jews for a river bank at the time when the Greek translators published their version, they thought that a bird accustomed to nest on river banks, that is, the charadrius, was called from it אגפה agapha, or rather agappa ^{R2}.

But the Arabs who translated it as parrot took the Aleph in the word אנפה anapha to stand for Ajin, so that it would be derived from ענף anaph, which means branch; and hence the name was given to the parrot, because it hangs its nest from the branches of trees ^{R3}. Cadamosto [=Alvise Cadamosto, Navigazioni (1455-56)], in chapter 30 of his Navigations: These birds have a wonderful skill and ingenuity in nest-building. For they seek out a very tall tree which has slender and thin twigs, scarcely able to bear any weight at all. To the tip of these they tie a hanging twig, from which they suspend the nest, built with wonderful industry, round like a ball, leaving only an opening, very narrow, which serves as a door. They say the bird does this to outwit the cunning of serpents. Gesner reports the very same from Petrus Gillius, page 723. And the Arabs attribute the same industry to the bird thenavvut. Alcamus: التنوط طاير يدلي خيوطا من شجرة وينسج عشه كقارورة الدهن منوطا بتلك الخيوط [al-tanawwuṭ ṭāʾir yudlī khuyūṭan min shajara wa-yansuju ʿushshahu ka-qārūrat al-duhn manūṭan bi-tilka al-khuyūṭ] Thenavvut (as if you were to say the hanging bird) is a certain bird which hangs a thread from a tree and weaves its nest like a flask of oil, suspended from that thread. Alasmius: انما سمي بذلك لانه يدلي خيطا من شجرة [innamā summiya bi-dhālika li-annahu yudlī khayṭan min shajara] [III, 105] يفرخ فيها [yufarrikhu fīhā] It is so called, namely, because it hangs a thread from the tree in which it nests; for نوط [nawṭ] means to hang. On the same bird Damir: من شانه انه اذا اقبل الليل اخذ بغصن شجرة ويضم عليه رجليه وينكس راسه ثم لا يزال يصبح حتي يطلع النور [min shaʾnihi annahu idhā aqbala al-layl akhadha bi-ghuṣn shajara wa-yaḍummu ʿalayhi rijlayhi wa-yunakkisu raʾsahu thumma lā yazālu yuṣbiḥu ḥattā yaṭluʿa al-nūr] It is its nature that, when night comes on, it takes hold of a branch of a tree, clasping its feet to it, with its head bent downward, and does not stop singing until day dawns ^{R4}. Amusing [col. 342] is what some add: وانما يفعل ذلك خوفا من السما تقع عليه [wa-innamā yafʿalu dhālika khawfan min al-samā taqaʿu ʿalayhi] that it does this lest the sky fall upon it. Like the Germans who, when asked by Alexander what they feared, answered that they feared only this, that the sky might fall. But, to return to the parrot: like the peacock, discussed above ^{e)}, I could hardly believe that the parrot was known to the Jews in the age of Moses. For it is an Indian bird. Writers testify to this with great agreement. Thus Ctesias writes in the Indica, as quoted by Photius, περὶ τοῦ ὀρνέου τοῦ βιττάκου, ὅτι γλῶσσαν ἀνθρωπίνην ἔχει, καὶ φωνὴν [peri tou orneou tou bittakou, hoti glōssan anthrōpinēn echei, kai phōnēn], concerning the bird bittacus, [III, 106] (as they then called it) that it has a human tongue and voice. Arrian also in the Indica: Σιττακοὺς δὲ Νέαρχος μὲν ὡς δή τι θαῦμα ἀπηγέεται, ὅτι γίγνονται ἐν τῇ Ἰνδῶν γῇ, καὶ ὁποῖος ὄρνις ἐστὶν ὁ σιττακὸς, καὶ ὅπως φωνὴν ἵει ἀνθρωπίνην [Sittakous de Nearchos men hōs dē ti thauma apēgeetai, hoti gignontai en tē Indōn gē, kai hopoios ornis estin ho sittakos, kai hopōs phōnēn hiei anthrōpinēn]. Nearchus (who campaigned with Alexander) relates as a kind of marvel that sittaci are born in India, and what sort of bird the sittacus is, and how it utters a human voice. From this you may gather that parrots were not yet known in Greece at that time. Aristotle, History, book 8, chapter 12: Καὶ τὸ Ἰνδικὸν ὄρνεον ἡ ψιττακὴ, τὸ λεγόμενον ἀνθρωπόγλωττον [Kai to Indikon orneon hē psittakē, to legomenon anthrōpoglōtton]; And the Indian bird, the parrot, which is said to have a human tongue. Pliny, book 10, chapter 42: India, however, sends this bird; it calls it psittace. Aelian, History, book 16, chapter 2: Ἐν Ἰνδοῖς μανθάνω σιττακοὺς ὄρνις γίνεσθαι [En Indois manthanō sittakous ornis ginesthai]. I hear that sittacus birds are bred among the Indians. See also book 13, chapter 18, and book 16, chapter 15. Pausanias in the Corinthiaca: Παρὰ δὲ Ἰνδῶν μόνων ἄλλα τε κομίζεται, καὶ ὄρνιθες οἱ ψιττακοί [Para de Indōn monōn alla te komizetai, kai ornithes hoi psittakoi]. From the Indians alone are brought both other things and parrots. Apuleius, Florida, book 2: The parrot is a bird of India. Solinus, chapter 52: India alone sends the parrot bird. Philostorgius, book 3, where he speaks of the lands lying toward the farthest East and South: Καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ τὴν σιττακὴν ἐκεῖθεν ἴσμεν νομιζομένην [Kai men dē kai tēn sittakēn ekeithen ismen nomizomenēn]; And indeed we know that the parrot too is brought from there. Hence Ovid, Amores, book 2, Elegy 6:
The parrot, a bird sent to me from the Eastern Indians.
Likewise,
The parrot, a gift given from the farthest edge of the world.
And Statius, book 2, Elegy 4:
That parrot, green ruler of the Eastern region.
And the old Poet in the Riddle On the Parrot:
The Indian land bore me on its purple shore, where the bright day returns as the orb is kindled.

Yet, to say nothing of the New World, modern voyages teach us that they are also brought from Africa, though from its interior. Nor had this escaped Pliny, who in book 6, chapter 29, in the itinerary from Syene to the island of Meroë published by Nero's scouts, describing the island of Gagaudes, says: there parrots were first seen. This is confirmed by Paulus Venetus [=Marco Polo], writing about Abasia in book 3, chapter 45: It has parrots and very beautiful epimachi. But I cannot at all make sense of these words of Diodorus, book 2, page 95: Αἱ δὲ τῆς Συρίας ἐσχατιαὶ ψιττακοὺς, καὶ πορφυρίωνας, καὶ μελεαγρίδας (ἐκτρέφουσι) [Hai de tēs Syrias eschatiai psittakous, kai porphyriōnas, kai meleagridas (ektrephousi)]. For it is a paradoxical claim, and indeed plainly false, that parrots are born in Syria. I therefore suspect that the passage is corrupt, although what should be restored does not occur to me.

notes.text: The Syriac Physiologus, edited by Tychsen, Chapter 15, also renders the Hebrew אנפה as charadrius, ܟܪܐܕܪܝܘܣ [כראדריוס]. He describes the bird as entirely white, with no blackness in it at all (ܐܝܬܝܗ ܚܘܪܬܐ ܟܠܗ ܘܠܝܬ ܒܗ ܐܘܟܡܘܬܐ ܡܕܡ [איתיה חורתא כלה ולית בה אוכמותא מדם]). "But among all the charadrii listed by Linnaeus, Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)], Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] and Buffon (says Tychsen in his Commentary on this Chapter, §. 2, p. 91), not a single one is found that is entirely white and could be reconciled with our author's charadrius. Moreover, nothing is found in this migratory bird for which it should be thought especially worthy of the company of princes."
notes.label: R2

notes.text: To me, however, Tychsen's conjecture seems closer to the truth: that the Arabs rendered the Hebrew אנפה as parrot, ببغا [bbghā], either because the Greek translators took χαραδριον [charadrion] to be a parrot, or because they sought help from the etymology. "For אנף means to breathe, to be angry, to snort with anger; and the parrot is not only by nature the most prone to anger of all birds, but when an unknown person approaches it, it usually snorts very fiercely, whether from anger, from aversion, or from fear."
notes.label: R3

notes.text: There can be no doubt that this bird is the Oriolus Galbula of Linnaeus (T. 1, vol. 1, p. 383, 13th ed.), or the picus nidum suspendens [woodpecker that suspends its nest] of Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)], Ornithol. vol. 1, book 12, p. 854 ff., which seems to be the same as Pliny's galgulus; his words in book 10, ch. 33 are: they affirm that the galguli themselves sleep hanging by their feet, because they hope they are safer that way. I shall add some passages from Aldrovandi to confirm and illustrate what Bochart has adduced from the Arabs. As I was eager, he says, to observe the skill which the bird is said to use in building its nest, behold, Cesare Rinaldi, a patrician of Bologna, opportunely sent me as a gift a nest found on his estate. This nest imitated a little bowl exactly: round, that is, and hollow, made entirely of hemp fibres, and attached at the top to a branch of a walnut tree already laden with fruit. To one who merely looks at it, its skill is not really apparent; but to one who examines it, nothing more ingenious seems possible to be made by a bird devoid of reason. For, wishing to build a nest of this kind, namely round and hollow, it had to search through many trees for a branch suitable for giving it that hemispherical shape; and being able to find one only in part, it chose among others this forked branch, because one of its forks, ending as it were in an elbow, came closer than the others to roundness. Nor does the whole skill depend on this, since it is far greater in the fastening of the hemp to the branches. For it is wound around them so ingeniously that you would think it made not by a bird but by men. But not even this will seem wonderful, if you hear what I am now going to say and examine closely how the whole hollow of the nest, hanging downward in the air, can support four young, and fairly large ones, indeed larger than adult sparrows, when, as I said, it consists entirely of prepared hemp, and that quite limp: so, lest this mishap should occur, the bird provided in this way: it strengthened the nest on the outside so excellently with certain thicker and stronger threads that it could be equal to a far heavier weight.
notes.label: R4
